fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds Into Each Project App
fields.features_subheading: Emergent builds project management automation as one app: the rules you write and the record they leave behind.
fields.feature_1:
Project rules written in plain English

Describe how work moves: who approves a request, which task waits on which, when the sponsor hears. Emergent builds the app and its database, and you change a rule by prompting.
fields.feature_2:
Reads the tracker you already use

The app connects to your project tracker and time tracking tool through their APIs. Task status and logged hours sync in, and new owners and due dates sync back to the tracker.
fields.feature_3:
Reminders that escalate on your clock

Choose when a reminder goes to a task owner in Slack or by email. Then set how many days late a task can run before the project lead gets an escalation naming the task and owner.
fields.feature_4:
Every project's history in one database

Every request and handoff is saved as a row in a database you own, with its logged hours. When a sponsor asks why a launch date moved, the answer is in the record, not in a thread.
fields.feature_5:
A portfolio board that updates live

The dashboard shows every active project with its next milestone, open tasks, and hours against budget. It updates as tasks close, so Monday's meeting starts from current numbers.
fields.feature_6:
Export the full code on paid plans

Export the project app's full code to your GitHub repository on paid plans. A developer can read how intake rules and budget alerts work and review each change like any other code.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Project Chores the App Takes Over
fields.tab_content_1:
Any request over 400 hours waits for the PMO lead

Bastian Ellerby at Brackenfield Logistics submits project request PR-214 for a customer portal, estimated at 520 hours. Any request over 400 hours needs the PMO lead's approval before work is scheduled. The app sends Philippa Tewkesbury a direct message with an Approve button and holds PR-214 in the intake queue.
fields.tab_content_2:
When the floor plans close, the structural review opens

Ingeborg Varnholt at Quillmoor Architects marks the floor plan revision done. The structural review cannot start until that task finishes. The app now assigns it to Corvin Teague. His direct message carries the revised drawings and a due date 5 working days out. The permit set waits on his review in turn.
fields.tab_content_3:
12 of 18 tasks done in Friday's report

Every Friday at 4 pm, the app reads the tracker for the Pennyroyal Orchard website rebuild and writes the status report. This week it shows 12 of 18 tasks done, with the content migration milestone 3 days late. The report goes by email to the sponsor, Margarethe Pelloux, and nobody copies numbers into a slide.
fields.tab_content_4:
The project lead hears first above 80% of the hours

Corrowind Studio's brand launch has a 300-hour budget, and the team has logged 246 of those hours. Once logged hours are over 80% of the budget, the app sends Leopold Winterbourne, the project lead, a direct message that shows 54 hours left. Its Review hours button opens the breakdown by person.

fields.howto_title: How to Build Project Management Automation
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to choose your first project management automation and test it on last month's projects before launch.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Pick the chore that repeats weekly
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Mark which tasks wait on others
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Write each rule with its number
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Map the fields each rule reads
fields.howto_step_1_des: List what your project leads did by hand last week: chasing approvals, reassigning work, building the status deck, and checking hours. Choose the one that comes back every week and ends the same way each time. Build that automation first.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Open your current project plan and mark every task that cannot start until another one finishes. In scheduling terms, that is a finish-to-start link. Write each one as a sentence, such as: when the floor plans are done, the structural review starts.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Give every rule a number anyone could check: requests over 400 hours go to the PMO lead, and the project lead hears once hours run above 80% of the budget. Describe the rules in a prompt, and Emergent builds the app around them.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Before you connect any tool, list the fields each rule depends on: task status, owner, due date, and logged hours. Check that people fill those fields in today, or the rule has nothing to act on.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Name a person for every alert
fields.howto_step_5_des: Decide who receives each message. The next task owner gets the handoff, the sponsor gets the Friday report, and the project lead gets the budget alert. Send escalations to a named person rather than a busy channel, where nobody owns the reply.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Load 2 projects you closed last month, with their real dates, owners, and hours. Mark one task done a day late and push one budget over its limit, then check that the handoff and the alert reach the right people. Fix any rule by prompting.
fields.howto_step_7_des: For the first 4 weeks, open the dashboard with your project leads each Monday. Note every alert that fired too early or too late and change its number. Add the next automation only when the first one runs without anyone stepping in.

faq_plan.a: Project management automation is the computerization of individual project management processes with specialized software, in Smartsheet's definition. Teams use it to schedule manual, repetitive tasks automatically based on predetermined triggers. On a live project, the trigger might be a task marked done or a Friday deadline.

faq_plan.q: How do I set up project management automation?
faq_plan.a: Write each rule down, connect the tools it reads, pick who gets each message, and test it on a finished project. With Emergent's AI automation builder, you describe each rule in plain English, and Emergent builds the app with its database and dashboard. You change any rule later by prompting.

faq_plan.q: What should stay manual in automated project management?
faq_plan.a: Keep the judgment calls manual: approving scope, trading a date against the budget, and telling a client about a slip. Automate what feeds those calls instead, such as the request that reaches the PMO lead with its estimate attached. A person still presses the Approve button; the app only makes sure the right person sees it on time.

faq_plan.q: What is the difference between AI and automation in project management?
faq_plan.ref: ai and automation in project management
faq_plan.secondary: ai and automation in project management
faq_plan.a: Automation follows rules you set, while AI handles the steps a fixed rule cannot, such as reading a statement of work. Plain task automation, like reassigning work when a task closes, needs no AI at all. An app Emergent builds can read documents into structured fields with AI and send any field it is unsure of to a person.

faq_plan.q: How do I choose project management automation tools?
faq_plan.a: Choose by testing each tool against the rules you already wrote. Check that it reads the fields those rules need from your tracker, and that it can message a named person rather than only a channel. Then compare what happens when runs exceed a plan's limit, which the table above lists. An app built with Emergent has no task cap.

faq_plan.q: Can project management automation write updates back to my tracker?
faq_plan.a: Yes, when the tracker has an API. The app Emergent builds connects to any tool with an API and syncs data in both directions, reading task status and writing back new owners and due dates. Before you plan a rule around a field, check that your tracker's API lets an outside app change it.

faq_plan.q: How should project management automation handle intake requests?
faq_plan.a: Give requesters one form with the fields the PMO needs to decide: the deliverable, the requested date, the hours estimate, and the sponsor. Route by estimate, sending large requests to the PMO lead. Send client support tickets to customer service automation instead, and keep this form for new work sized in hours. Review the routing rules each quarter.

faq_plan.q: How often should project management automation send status reports?
faq_plan.a: Send them weekly while a project is active, and give executives a monthly summary with only the milestones. Fix the time, such as Friday afternoon, so sponsors know when to look. In Smartsheet's words, one of the most commonly automated tasks is the compiling and sharing of status reports.

faq_plan.q: How do I tell if project management automation is working?
faq_plan.a: Measure two numbers before and after launch: how long a handoff waits between one task closing and the next owner starting, and how many hours project leads spend building reports. Watch the weekly count of escalations too. A rising count points to a rule set too tight or an owner with too much work.

faq_plan.q: How should project management automation handle a blocked task?
faq_plan.a: Treat a blocked task as an alert with an owner. When someone marks a task blocked, have the app message the person who can clear it and start an escalation clock. Route production outages to incident response automation instead. Keep project escalations to working hours, and page nobody at night over a blocked task.

plan.angle: The top 10 are vendor blogs and listicles that explain project management automation in general terms and list tasks worth automating. This page shows four automations a project team runs every week as working screens: an oversized project request routed to the PMO lead at 400 hours, a structural review assigned the moment the floor plans it depends on are done, a Friday status report built from the tracker, and a budget alert at 80% of the hours. The FAQ answers what searchers compare: how to set it up, where AI fits, which tools to pick and what to automate first.
